listenings.text: Here is something most executives get wrong about accent. The people in the room are not judging where you are from. They are trying to find the important word in your sentence, and they find it by listening for stress. In a room with investors from Toronto, Madrid, Abu Dhabi and Shanghai, English is almost everyone's second language, so the risk is not your accent. The risk is a flat sentence, where every syllable weighs the same and the key word disappears. Three habits fix most of it. Slow down on the numbers and the names. Put the stress where the dictionary puts it, especially on the long words of your industry. And pause before the idea you want people to remember, not after it. Nobody in that room needs you to sound American. They need to know which word matters.

Good evening, and thank you for staying after a long day. There are about a hundred and forty people in this room tonight, and roughly a third of you manage somebody else's retirement, so I will keep this short. Tomorrow morning we will talk about numbers. Tonight I want to talk about trust. In the next hour you will hear from two toll road operators, one regulator and a sovereign wealth fund, and I have asked each of them to answer one question only: what would make you sign a thirty-year contract in this region? All I ask from the rest of you is simple. When you disagree, say so on stage, not in the corridor. That is the conversation this dinner exists for.
